title: SPECIAL REPORT: Inside AI scam ads exploiting TikTok’s advertising system to defraud Nigerians

reading.body:
This is a case of impersonation carried out through a platform's paid advertising system. The ads used deepfake video and cloned voices to present themselves as banks, telecoms companies and named public figures, and they ran as promotions inside TikTok's ad delivery rather than as ordinary posts. The harm occurred at the point of payment, after victims submitted account details or transferred cryptocurrency in response to offers of grants, loans and investment returns.

The failure mode is a system that accepted and distributed paid content without verifying who was behind it. The ads were written in multiple languages, disabled comments and carried no AI labels, which reduced the chances of either the platform or other users flagging them. Catching this would have required advertiser identity checks before the ads ran, and detection aimed at impersonation of specific brands and public figures rather than at scam content in general.

It is not established that TikTok knew the ads were fraudulent, and the article's finding of moderation gaps is a reporting finding, not an adjudicated one. TikTok was asked for comment, and no response or subsequent action by the company is recorded in the available facts.

reports.title: SPECIAL REPORT: Inside AI scam ads exploiting TikTok’s advertising system to defraud Nigerians

summary:
A Premium Times investigation found that AI-generated scam ads are running as paid promotions on TikTok and defrauding Nigerians. Scammers impersonate brands such as OPay, UBA, MTN and Airtel, and public figures including Aliko Dangote and Tony Elumelu, using deepfake videos and cloned voices to promise grants, loans and investment returns. One victim, Mohammed Yusuf, lost about N150,000 after submitting his OPay details, and Ahmad Wura lost roughly N1 million in cryptocurrency. The reporter archived 130 such ads over five weeks, with OPay impersonated in 28 of them.

The ads appeared in English, Pidgin, Yoruba and Hausa, often disabled comments and carried no AI labels. TikTok’s policies ban scams and impersonation, but the investigation found moderation gaps, and the article says TikTok was asked for comment. Experts called for stronger advertiser checks and proactive Nigerian laws holding platforms to higher standards.
